screens.title: Project 9 — The Operating System and Integration
screens.narratorSegment: This final project ties together everything you've built across the course. You will complete the Jack operating system, test each OS service with the supplied test programs, and run a complete application — Tetris — on the machine you constructed. That single Nand gate you started with now underpins a complete layered stack: hardware, assembler, VM translator, compiler, and OS. In concrete terms, the OS implements modules such as Memory, Array, Math, String, Output, Screen, Keyboard and Sys. You will test each module with programs like MemoryTest and Pong, and finally boot the system to run Tetris. This moment matters because it converts fragmented skills into integrated systems thinking. You will see how low-level choices influence higher-level behavior, how bootstrap code hands control to Sys. init, and how the OS provides services the game relies on. As you explore, notice which module gave you the most friction and why that reveals the hidden complexity of system software. What insight will you carry forward from this final integration?

Module 8 › Chapter: Project 9 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Project 9 — OS & Integration

Complete the Jack OS modules and run the full stack so the Hack computer can boot and execute Tetris. This is the final integration: hardware, toolchain, compiler, and OS working together.

In this lesson: finish OS modules, run tests, bootstrap Sys.init, and play Tetris as proof of a working stack.
Explore Key Topics
OS modules: Memory, Array, Math, String, Output, Screen, Keyboard, Sys — implement and test each service.
Boot sequence: bootstrap initializes the stack pointer and transfers control to Sys.init, which initializes services and calls Main.main.
Testing & verification: run MemoryTest, MathTest, ScreenTest, Pong and Tetris to validate the full system.
Visual Concept
Hardware
Nand → CPU → Memory
Toolchain
Assembler → VM translator → Compiler
OS & Apps
Jack OS services → Tetris
These cards represent the layers you built. Each layer abstracts the one below it. When they integrate correctly, the top-level program runs unchanged on the hardware you designed.
Coming up

What you'll do next

Complete the OS modules, run the tests provided, and boot the simulator to play Tetris. Document your experience and reflect on the architecture choices you made.

This screen introduces the final integration. Use it as your map for the remaining steps.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of Project 9 you will have completed four tangible outcomes. First, you will finish the Jack OS implementation so it provides the services that higher-level programs rely on. This means implementing Memory, Array, Math, String, Output, Screen, Keyboard and Sys modules according to the project specification. Second, you will test the OS with the provided Jack programs, running each test to verify behavior and diagnosing mismatches. Third, you will boot the full stack to run a complex application like Tetris, observing how bootstrap code and Sys. init hand control to Main. main. Fourth, you will reflect on the entire Nand2Tetris journey: how low-level decisions affect high-level behavior and what abstractions made the work manageable. Each objective is both practical and reflective: you will ship working code, run a full-system test, observe runtime behavior, and write a considered reflection that ties implementation choices back to systems principles. These skills show you can engineer and reason about an entire computing stack.

screens.title: Skills and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on methods and evidence: what you will run and what to inspect when things go wrong. You will use the provided Jack test programs as a checklist. MemoryTest verifies allocation and deallocation; MathTest and StringTest confirm your helper routines; KeyboardTest and ScreenTest validate input and output; OutputTest checks text output. Most importantly, run Pong and Tetris as system-level checks. When a test fails, isolate whether the issue is in the OS service implementation, in calling conventions from compiled code, or in the translator/assembler output. A common pitfall is assuming higher-level semantics without confirming calling protocols at the VM/assembly boundary. Your verification should include step-by-step reproduction: run a test, observe failing behaviors in the simulator, inspect memory/state traces, and then fix the module. Document the steps, recording the failing input, the observed output, and the fix you applied. This traceable evidence is how you demonstrate competency.

content.html:
Module 8 › Project 9 › Verification
Test Suite
  • MemoryTest — allocation and deallocation checks.
  • MathTest & StringTest — library routines and edge cases.
  • KeyboardTest & ScreenTest — I/O and display correctness.
  • Pong & Tetris — final system-level integration and performance checks.
Troubleshooting Pattern
  1. Run the failing test and capture the simulator trace.
  2. Identify whether the bug is in an OS service or earlier toolchain output.
  3. Reproduce with a minimal input and inspect memory and register state.
  4. Apply a focused fix, re-run tests, and document the change.
Tip: keep small, reproducible test cases to avoid chasing unrelated failures.

screens.title: What Project 9 Requires: Complete the Jack OS
screens.narratorSegment: Project 9 asks you to implement a small but complete operating system in Jack. The OS is not a full modern kernel; it's a set of modules that provide services higher-level programs expect. Implementations include Memory for allocation and deallocation; Array for building and freeing arrays; Math for helper numerical functions; String for textual operations; Output for text output; Screen for graphics; Keyboard for input; and Sys for bootstrapping and system services. Each module exposes a compact A P I that the compiled game or tests call. For example, Memory manages pointers and free lists, which higher-level code uses without knowing the physical layout. A common misconception is that OS modules are independent — in practice they interact: Array relies on Memory, Screen relies on Output primitives, and Sys ties them together at startup. Your task is to make these contracts precise and reliable. Implementing them successfully demonstrates mastery of abstraction: you will make small, testable services that together enable complex applications like Tetris. Which module will teach you the most about abstraction? What Project 9 Requires: Complete the Jack OS means the jack os is a set of focused service modules. each module hides low-level details and offers primitives used by applications and tests.. In practical terms, understand each os module and its role in the layered stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: OS as service collection
keyIdea.text: The Jack OS is a set of focused service modules. Each module hides low-level details and offers primitives used by applications and tests.

content.html:
Core Concept › OS Modules
Module Definitions
  • Memory — allocation and deallocation primitives for the heap.
  • Array — constructs and disposes variable-length arrays using Memory.
  • Math & String — helper functions used by higher-level code.
  • Output, Screen, Keyboard — I/O primitives for text, graphics, and input.
  • Sys — bootstrap and system-level services that initialize the OS.
Concrete example
When Tetris needs a board, Main.main calls Array to allocate the board. Array uses Memory to reserve space and returns a pointer. Later, when a level ends, Array calls Memory to free the space. The OS modules coordinate to make this safe and predictable.
Common misconception
Students sometimes treat OS modules as independent libraries. In practice, they form a small ecosystem. If Memory semantics change, Array and Sys must adapt. Treat module interfaces as contracts and test them in isolation and in integration.
Key Takeaway

Design clear module contracts and verify both unit behavior and system integration to ensure Tetris runs on your stack.

screens.title: OS Module Implementation Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Approach each OS module with a repeatable process: specification, implementation, unit test, integration test, then documentation. Start by reading the exact module specification to know which functions and semantics you must provide. Implement the smallest correct behavior first — minimal allocations for Memory, a basic array constructor for Array, simple character output for Output. Next, write or run the supplied unit tests like MemoryTest or MathTest to confirm basic behavior. Then integrate the module into the running stack and exercise it with higher-level programs, observing interactions that unit tests might miss. For example, a Memory implementation that passes allocation tests might still leak when arrays are repeatedly created and freed under game load. Document any assumptions and edge cases you handled: pointer alignment, error returns, and expected free behavior. Finally, run a system test (Pong or Tetris) as the final integration gate. This pattern reduces debugging time because you detect incorrect assumptions early and build confidence through progressively broader tests. OS Module Implementation Steps means implement modules incrementally: spec, minimal implementation, unit test, integrate, system test, and document assumptions.. In practical terms, a step-by-step pattern to implement and verify each os module. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Build and Verify
Step-by-step cards
  1. Read the spec: capture function signatures and edge cases.
  2. Implement minimal behavior: make the simplest correct code pass basic checks.
  3. Run unit tests: use provided tests to validate correctness.
  4. Integrate and stress: run Pong or repeated allocations to reveal leaks.
  5. Document assumptions: record alignment, pointer semantics and error handling.
Concrete scenario

If Array.free fails under sustained use, reproduce with a small loop that allocates and frees many arrays, inspect MemoryTest traces to find an inconsistent free path, and then fix the bookkeeping in Memory or Array accordingly.

Common mistake
Rushing to integrate before passing unit tests often leads to hard-to-track failures. Unit tests catch contract violations; run them frequently as you change code.
Key Takeaway

An incremental, test-driven process reduces integration surprises and helps isolate bugs to a single module or interaction.

screens.title: Memory Module Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: The Memory module is the backbone of the Jack OS: it supplies allocation and deallocation primitives used by Array and many higher-level routines. A correct Memory implementation must manage a heap region, maintain pointers to free blocks, and return stable addresses to callers. In this environment, 'allocation' means reserving a contiguous block of words and returning its base address; 'deallocation' means returning the block for reuse. A concrete example: when the Tetris game requests a new game board, it asks the OS for a block large enough to hold the board state; Memory reserves space and returns a pointer the compiler-generated code will use. A common pitfall is pointer misuse: assuming freed memory remains valid. That causes use-after-free bugs that only appear under repeated allocation patterns, such as long-running games. To test Memory, run MemoryTest and also stress the allocation/free cycle while running Pong or Tetris. The final insight is practical: correct memory semantics make every other module simpler because you can depend on allocation guarantees. Memory Module Deep Dive means memory must provide reliable allocation and deallocation so higher-level modules can build arrays and data structures without low-level leaks or corruption.. In practical terms, allocation, deallocation, and the expectations of the memory api. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Memory Module
What Memory provides
  • Allocate(size): reserve a contiguous block of words and return its base address.
  • Free(address): release a previously allocated block so it can be reused.
  • Stability: addresses remain valid until freed; freed memory must not be used.
Test: run MemoryTest and then a stress loop that allocates and frees repeatedly to reveal leaks.
Concrete example

When the game allocates a board: Array calls Memory.allocate(size). Memory returns pointer X. The compiled code stores and manipulates data at X. If Memory.free(X) is later called, any subsequent read at X is undefined. Reproduce such errors by looping allocate/free and then checking the board contents after re-allocation.

Common mistake
Treating freed memory as implicitly zeroed or preserved. Memory reuses blocks; do not rely on prior contents after allocation.

screens.title: Array Module and Memory Interaction
screens.narratorSegment: The Array module provides a higher-level abstraction for variable-length collections built on Memory. Its responsibilities include creating arrays with a requested size, providing indexed access, and freeing the memory when the array is no longer needed. Concretely, an array constructor calls Memory. allocate to reserve a block that contains metadata (length) followed by array elements. Indexed access is then performed by computing element offsets from the returned base pointer. The Array. free routine must return the entire block correctly to Memory. free. A typical bug arises when indexing arithmetic is off by one or when metadata layout assumptions differ between Array and the code that reads arrays. Test Array thoroughly with StringTest and programs that build, mutate, and free arrays in loops. Understand that Array is a thin wrapper: its correctness depends directly on Memory semantics. If Memory provides stable, consistent allocations, Array can be simple and reliable; if Memory misbehaves, array-level bugs proliferate. The learning point is to validate the interface between these two modules with small, focused tests. Array Module and Memory Interaction means array uses memory.allocate and memory.free; verify layout and indexing assumptions to avoid off-by-one and use-after-free bugs.. In practical terms, how arrays are constructed, used, and freed on top of memory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Array & Memory
Array layout
  1. Array.allocate(n) calls Memory.allocate(n + metadata) and returns base pointer.
  2. Element i is stored at base + metadata + i.
  3. Array.free(base) calls Memory.free with the original block address.
Example scenario

A Tetris piece list might be stored in an array. The game allocates the array, updates positions frequently, and finally frees it between levels. If indexing is wrong, pieces corrupt the board state; reproduce with short sequences of allocations and element writes.

Key Takeaway

Keep layout contracts explicit between Array and Memory and test both unit and integration behavior under repeated allocations.

screens.title: Math, String, and Output Services
screens.narratorSegment: Math, String, and Output are utility modules that simplify common tasks for programs like Tetris. Math exposes helper functions used by game logic, such as arithmetic operations too verbose to write inline in Jack. String offers operations for building and inspecting text, which is useful for status messages and debugging output. Output provides text printing routines that higher-level code uses to show scores or messages. Together these modules are less structural than Memory or Array, but they matter because they encapsulate recurring logic and improve readability. For example, Tetris might call Output. printString to display the current level; that routine depends on String utilities to format the text. A misconception is to under-test these helpers because they seem trivial; in long-running applications, small math or string bugs accumulate into visible glitches. Test them with MathTest and StringTest and exercise Output with OutputTest. Keep these modules simple and well-documented so the compiler-generated code and runtime agree on calling conventions and return values. Math, String, and Output Services means math, string, and output reduce repetitive code and must be correct because many higher-level behaviors depend on them.. In practical terms, small libraries that simplify higher-level code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Helpers vs Services
Math

Small numeric helpers used by game logic; speeds development and keeps compiled code tidy.

String

String construction and inspection routines used by Output and debugging messages.

Output

Text printing primitives used to show scores and status messages; validate with OutputTest.

Concrete check
Run MathTest and StringTest to check edge cases. Then run OutputTest to ensure printed strings render correctly to the simulator. Small helper bugs can create confusing higher-level failures, so test early.

screens.title: Screen and Keyboard: I/O Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Screen and Keyboard modules connect the virtual machine to the outside world. The Screen module exposes drawing primitives the game uses to render blocks and the playfield; the Keyboard module supplies input events. Architecturally, Screen writes to memory-mapped display locations or calls provided output routines that the simulator translates into pixels, while Keyboard reads a buffered input state supplied by the simulator. A concrete sequence: the game computes new piece positions, calls Screen. draw to update pixels, and then polls Keyboard. read to handle player input. A frequent misconception is treating input and output as instantaneous and lossless; in practice input may be buffered and display updates can be batched. Test these modules with ScreenTest and KeyboardTest, and then validate under gameplay in Pong or Tetris to ensure the update rate and input latency meet expectations. The key design goal is simple, predictable primitives that the compiler and runtime agree on so user interactions feel correct during play. Screen and Keyboard: I/O Architecture means screen updates and keyboard input provide the runtime bridge to interactive programs; verify behavior under realistic game conditions.. In practical terms, how graphics output and input flow through the os. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture › I/O Modules
Screen
Provides drawing primitives used by games to render shapes and the board. Implementations map drawing calls to simulator display memory or output routines. Test with ScreenTest and verify refresh behavior during gameplay.
Keyboard

screens.title: Bootstrapping and the Complete Stack
screens.narratorSegment: When you run Tetris on the completed system, a precise sequence of events ties all layers together. First, the Computer Simulator loads the machine code for Tetris into ROM. Next, the bootstrap code executes: it initializes the stack pointer and calls Sys. init. Sys. init is the OS entry point that initializes services like Memory, Math, Output, Screen and Keyboard, setting up any required runtime state. After that, control transfers to Main. main, the game entry point produced by the Jack compiler. The running game now uses the OS services for memory allocation, drawing, and input handling. A concrete observation: if the bootstrap fails to set the stack pointer correctly, compiled code will corrupt memory at first call and tests will fail immediately. Similarly, if Sys. init does not initialize Output or Screen correctly, Tetris may run but not render. Testing at each transfer point — after bootstrap, after Sys. init, and after Main. main — helps localize faults. This stack demonstrates the central lesson of the course: simple hardware plus layered software yields expressive computing power. Bootstrapping and the Complete Stack means boot: load machine code, run bootstrap to init sp, call sys.init to configure os, then run main.main — this sequence ties hardware to application.. In practical terms, follow the execution path when tetris runs on your machine. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing the OS with Provided Programs
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is the evidence that your OS works. Begin with unit tests like MemoryTest, MathTest and StringTest. These confirm that each service implements the required semantics. When a unit test fails, use the simulator's tracing and memory-view features to inspect addresses, register contents, and stack frames. If unit tests pass, move to integration tests: KeyboardTest and ScreenTest for input and output, OutputTest for text, and then Pong as a mid-level game. Pong reveals timing and interactive behaviors before you attempt Tetris. The final tests are Pong and Tetris: they exercise long-running allocation patterns, repeated rendering, and sustained input handling. A typical debugging pattern is to reproduce the failing behavior with the smallest possible program, capture the simulator trace where control flows from VM/assembly into OS calls, and compare actual state to expected values. Document your fixes: which test failed, what you observed, what you changed, and why the change is correct. This disciplined trace-record-fix loop is how you deliver a robust OS. screens.title: Reflecting on the Journey: From Nand to Tetris

fullNarratorScript:
This final project ties together everything you've built across the course. You will complete the Jack operating system, test each OS service with the supplied test programs, and run a complete application — Tetris — on the machine you constructed. That single Nand gate you started with now underpins a complete layered stack: hardware, assembler, VM translator, compiler, and OS. In concrete terms, the OS implements modules such as Memory, Array, Math, String, Output, Screen, Keyboard and Sys. You will test each module with programs like MemoryTest and Pong, and finally boot the system to run Tetris. This moment matters because it converts fragmented skills into integrated systems thinking. You will see how low-level choices influence higher-level behavior, how bootstrap code hands control to Sys. init, and how the OS provides services the game relies on. As you explore, notice which module gave you the most friction and why that reveals the hidden complexity of system software. What insight will you carry forward from this final integration?

By the end of Project 9 you will have completed four tangible outcomes. First, you will finish the Jack OS implementation so it provides the services that higher-level programs rely on. This means implementing Memory, Array, Math, String, Output, Screen, Keyboard and Sys modules according to the project specification. Second, you will test the OS with the provided Jack programs, running each test to verify behavior and diagnosing mismatches. Third, you will boot the full stack to run a complex application like Tetris, observing how bootstrap code and Sys. init hand control to Main. main. Fourth, you will reflect on the entire Nand2Tetris journey: how low-level decisions affect high-level behavior and what abstractions made the work manageable. Each objective is both practical and reflective: you will ship working code, run a full-system test, observe runtime behavior, and write a considered reflection that ties implementation choices back to systems principles. These skills show you can engineer and reason about an entire computing stack.

This second objectives slide focuses on methods and evidence: what you will run and what to inspect when things go wrong. You will use the provided Jack test programs as a checklist. MemoryTest verifies allocation and deallocation; MathTest and StringTest confirm your helper routines; KeyboardTest and ScreenTest validate input and output; OutputTest checks text output. Most importantly, run Pong and Tetris as system-level checks. When a test fails, isolate whether the issue is in the OS service implementation, in calling conventions from compiled code, or in the translator/assembler output. A common pitfall is assuming higher-level semantics without confirming calling protocols at the VM/assembly boundary. Your verification should include step-by-step reproduction: run a test, observe failing behaviors in the simulator, inspect memory/state traces, and then fix the module. Document the steps, recording the failing input, the observed output, and the fix you applied. This traceable evidence is how you demonstrate competency.

Project 9 asks you to implement a small but complete operating system in Jack. The OS is not a full modern kernel; it's a set of modules that provide services higher-level programs expect. Implementations include Memory for allocation and deallocation; Array for building and freeing arrays; Math for helper numerical functions; String for textual operations; Output for text output; Screen for graphics; Keyboard for input; and Sys for bootstrapping and system services. Each module exposes a compact A P I that the compiled game or tests call. For example, Memory manages pointers and free lists, which higher-level code uses without knowing the physical layout. A common misconception is that OS modules are independent — in practice they interact: Array relies on Memory, Screen relies on Output primitives, and Sys ties them together at startup. Your task is to make these contracts precise and reliable. Implementing them successfully demonstrates mastery of abstraction: you will make small, testable services that together enable complex applications like Tetris. Which module will teach you the most about abstraction? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Start by reading the exact module specification to know which functions and semantics you must provide. Implement the smallest correct behavior first — minimal allocations for Memory, a basic array constructor for Array, simple character output for Output. Next, write or run the supplied unit tests like MemoryTest or MathTest to confirm basic behavior. Then integrate the module into the running stack and exercise it with higher-level programs, observing interactions that unit tests might miss. For example, a Memory implementation that passes allocation tests might still leak when arrays are repeatedly created and freed under game load. Document any assumptions and edge cases you handled: pointer alignment, error returns, and expected free behavior. Finally, run a system test (Pong or Tetris) as the final integration gate. This pattern reduces debugging time because you detect incorrect assumptions early and build confidence through progressively broader tests. The Memory module is the backbone of the Jack OS: it supplies allocation and deallocation primitives used by Array and many higher-level routines. A correct Memory implementation must manage a heap region, maintain pointers to free blocks, and return stable addresses to callers. In this environment, 'allocation' means reserving a contiguous block of words and returning its base address; 'deallocation' means returning the block for reuse. A concrete example: when the Tetris game requests a new game board, it asks the OS for a block large enough to hold the board state; Memory reserves space and returns a pointer the compiler-generated code will use. A common pitfall is pointer misuse: assuming freed memory remains valid. That causes use-after-free bugs that only appear under repeated allocation patterns, such as long-running games. To test Memory, run MemoryTest and also stress the allocation/free cycle while running Pong or Tetris. The final insight is practical: correct memory semantics make every other module simpler because you can depend on allocation guarantees. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The Array module provides a higher-level abstraction for variable-length collections built on Memory. Its responsibilities include creating arrays with a requested size, providing indexed access, and freeing the memory when the array is no longer needed. Concretely, an array constructor calls Memory. allocate to reserve a block that contains metadata (length) followed by array elements. Indexed access is then performed by computing element offsets from the returned base pointer. The Array. free routine must return the entire block correctly to Memory. free. A typical bug arises when indexing arithmetic is off by one or when metadata layout assumptions differ between Array and the code that reads arrays. Test Array thoroughly with StringTest and programs that build, mutate, and free arrays in loops. Understand that Array is a thin wrapper: its correctness depends directly on Memory semantics. If Memory provides stable, consistent allocations, Array can be simple and reliable; if Memory misbehaves, array-level bugs proliferate. The learning point is to validate the interface between these two modules with small, focused tests. Output provides text printing routines that higher-level code uses to show scores or messages. Together these modules are less structural than Memory or Array, but they matter because they encapsulate recurring logic and improve readability.
